definition.text: A rule in optimal control theory for finding the best way to steer a dynamical system from one state to another, especially when states or controls are constrained.

facts.text: It says an optimal control and its state path must solve the Hamiltonian system, a two-point boundary value problem, and maximize the control Hamiltonian.
Lev Pontryagin and his students formulated it in 1956; its first use was maximizing a rocket's final speed.
Its power is that maximizing the Hamiltonian at each moment is much easier than optimizing over whole functions.
The conditions are necessary, and become sufficient under certain convexity conditions.
Unlike the Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman equation, which must hold over the whole state space, its conditions need only hold along one path, which can make it more efficient to compute.
In differential games, open-loop strategies are found with the maximum principle and closed-loop strategies with dynamic programming.

title: Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman equation

definition.text: The partial differential equation that plays the role of the Bellman equation in continuous-time optimization problems.

facts.text: Solving it gives a sufficient condition for an optimal control, while Pontryagin's principle gives a necessary one.
It provides a necessary and sufficient condition for an optimum and extends easily to stochastic optimal control problems.
It is used to find optimal policies in continuous-time Markov decision processes with continuous states and actions.

notes: No article of its own crawled; passes test 5 (Bellman equation, Dynamic programming, Optimal control, Pontryagin's maximum principle, Markov decision process).

definition.text: The study of whether the solutions of differential equations and the paths of dynamical systems stay close when their starting conditions are disturbed slightly.

facts.text: It asks whether a nearby path will stay close to a given one forever, and whether it will converge to it.
An equilibrium is stable if starting close keeps a system close, and asymptotically stable if the system also returns to it over time.
A key idea is to analyze behaviour near an equilibrium by linearizing the system, where eigenvalues of a matrix describe how nearby points move.
If all eigenvalues have negative real parts, the point is a stable attracting fixed point that nearby points approach at an exponential rate.
In economics, a price adjusting to excess demand converges to equilibrium only if the derivative of its rate of change with respect to price is negative.
Stability can also be applied to Nash equilibria; Cournot introduced best-response dynamics in studying the stability of equilibrium.

definition.text: An equilibrium is stable if a small push leads only to small, local movement, and unstable if a small push can send the system far away.

facts.text: A pendulum shows stable equilibrium with small oscillations; a ball resting on top of a hill shows unstable equilibrium.
With damping, a stable equilibrium is also asymptotically stable.
For an iterated map, a fixed point is stable if the derivative there is less than 1 in absolute value and unstable if greater.

title: Lyapunov function
article: Stability theory#Lyapunov function for general dynamical systems

definition.text: A function of a system's state whose existence demonstrates that the system is stable.

facts.text: Lyapunov functions are a general way to prove that a dynamical system is stable or asymptotically stable.
It is often useful to picture a Lyapunov function as the energy of the system.
Aleksandr Lyapunov showed in 1892 that systems of ordinary differential equations behave stably given a suitable Lyapunov function.

title: Steady state

definition.text: The condition of a system whose defining variables are not changing over time.

facts.text: In continuous time the rate of change of each property is zero; in discrete time each period-to-period difference is zero.
Many systems pass through a transient, warm-up period before reaching steady state, and often only approach it gradually.
A reservoir in a biogeochemical box model is in steady state when its sources balance its sinks.
In the Solow–Swan growth model, the steady state is reached when gross investment in physical capital equals depreciation.
Exogenous growth models without technological change predict that economies converge to a steady state with zero per-capita growth.
A steady-state economy has a stable population and stable consumption at or below carrying capacity.
An unstable system moves away from its steady state.
